Zak Helenske, Three Lidded Jars





     Zak Helenske, Bowl

Zak Helenske, Bowl, photos courtesy of the artist

Please tell us about your process.
For these constructed vessels, I begin by throwing parts on the wheel. These are usually
cone-shaped bowls, sometimes with lids. I have found that I prefer these thrown shapes to
be less volumetric and more geometric. After throwing a batch of parts, I pound out slabs.
I use a flat wooden mallet to make my slabs and a long metal ruler to compress. I have an
idea of the shapes I will cut, but after the first few, I diverge and allow myself to explore
new shapes.
  Once the horizontal and vertical planes are established, I measure the diameter of the
bowl. I cut the appropriate-sized circle out of the center with help of the spinning wheel.
Next, I attach the bowl to the horizontal plane, keeping it flat and upside down. Then, I
attach the vertical support. In order to maintain a 90-degree angle, I use scraps of slabs cut
to 90 degrees as buttresses, which keeps the vertical slab straight while it dries. Ideally, I
am working with the slabs somewhere between soft and hard. Once constructed, I let the
forms dry under plastic, keeping them upside down for a couple of days. When I flip them,
I clean any seams that were hidden and level the vertical support to the bowl.

What are you inspired or inﬂuenced by?
Originally, this form was inspired by a show of Isamu Noguchi’s “Playscapes.” The show
was comprised of drawings and models, and I was taken by the long shadows cast from the

geometric shapes of his playgrounds. The geometry of the slabs rests upon or sometimes
intersects, the vessel to create an architecture around the bowl. I build the forms upside
down; they resemble architectural models at this stage, which I like.
  The objects I make describe a connection between architecture and our haptic
experience. When making pottery, I think about my blind grandparents, and how they
would trace their surroundings with their fingertips. Their haptic experience was of
necessity, navigating their world without sight. I imagine my work living at our human scale,
able to be navigated with our fingertips.

PROJECT:
                 Juicer

One of my favorite shapes to make is the citrus juicer! You never know
when you are going to need a squeeze of lemon, lime, mandarin, or
grapefruit in a recipe. Shifting the size of the reamer and strainer holes will
affect the pulp level, so make a few and see what suits your taste. Make
sure to use a hard, shiny glaze for the reamer, as it will need to withstand
acidic juice.
    It is interesting to make a shape that has such a specific use. I find the
challenge of inventing a form around a particular use pushes me to discover
new combinations. When I bring these combinations into other forms, it
helps my whole body of work evolve forward.

Tools & Materials
basic tool kit

Clay prepared as follows:
For reamer: 1/3 lb. (151 g) clay, domed closed form (shown here), 21/2" diameter by 21/2"
    tall (6.5 cm × 6.5 cm) dried to leather-hard
For wall: 1/2 lb. (226 g) clay, bottomless cylinder (soft leather-hard), 2" tall × 6" diameter
   (5 cm × 15 cm)
For the foot, spout, and handle: 10" × 10" × 1/4" (25.5 cm × 25.5 cm × 6 mm) thick soft
   leather-hard slab

Templates:
Spout Template
Handle Templates A, B, and C
Wall Dart Template

interfacing
MK3 (quilting tool for measuring cut marks)
banding wheel

water or slip for attachments





Instructions

Altering the Wall
Let’s jump right in! I recommend working on a banding wheel for the
assembly of all these pieces. Place the 6" (15 cm) diameter wall on a piece
of interfacing on your banding wheel. Shape it into a teardrop shape by

pressing the heels of your hands together at one end, creating a point. This
is where the handle will go. [A]





   Currently, the rim of the wall should be level with the working surface.
You are going to change the movement of the wall by removing clay from
the bottom. (Removing it from the top would ruin the finished rim.) This
alteration will transform the wall from a horizontal orientation to a softly
curving rim. Align the dart template and transfer it to both sides of the wall,
making sure the wider part of the curve corresponds to the point of the
teardrop shape. Cut along these lines and remove the clay. [B] Now this is
the tricky part: the next step is to bend and stretch the clay downward until
it is flat against the working surface. If you do this too fast, or put all the
pressure in one area, the wall will crack. Go slow and try to distribute the
pressure evenly. When you are done, the bottom edge of the wall should
touch the working surface all the way around. [C]

Adding the Texture to the Reamer
The sharper the edges on your reamer, the more pulp it will remove. There
are so many ways to create texture on the reamer, including carving, slip
trailing, altering on the wheel, pressing the clay into a mold, and more. I use
a dividing tool to mark out the number of lines I want to carve. [D]





  Hold a knife at an angle and cut a curving line up the reamer from the
foot. Now flip the reamer orientation to your cutting hand and cut along the
same line at a perpendicular angle to the first to remove a curving wedge of
clay. [E] Repeat this process as you work around the reamer. Run a wooden
smoothing tool along the corner of these cuts. Then add a tiny ball of clay
right at the tip of the reamer. Finish by smoothing the surface with a
sponge. It is much easier to smooth the reamer at this stage than to wait
until after it is tucked down inside the walls.

Assembling the Juicer
Place the altered wall on a slab and trace around the bottom. Cut out the
slab, trimming slightly outside the traced line. Now score the edges along
the bottom of the wall and the attachment area on the surface of the slab and
attach them together. Center the reamer within the wall on the slab foot.
Trace around its foot then set the reamer aside. Cut away the center,
working 1/4" (6 mm) away from the traced line towards the center. Run a
coil all along the inside of the teardrop-shaped wall, creating a rounded
interior corner. (This helps with cleaning as well as making it stronger). [F]

Score the edges of the closed form/reamer and the slab foot and attach
them. Smooth and compress the seam around the reamer with a rib tool.
Wait to smooth the seam underneath until the slab is a very firm leather-
hard to avoid stressing seams and causing warping.

Adding the Appendages
Using the Spout and Handle Templates, cut out the pieces for your juicer.
Hold the spout up to the curve of the wall. Trace around the spout. [G] This
line will give you a guide for cutting out the holes to trap the citrus seeds
(very important!). You can play with pattern or the shape of your holes to
take your juicer to the next level. Use a sponge or paintbrush to clean up
any burs on the holes, as it is hard to do this once the spout is in place.

Attach the spout by slipping and scoring both edges and pressing it into
place. [H] Now check out the angle of your spout. Do you want to change it?
You still can! You can take a dart out of the spout to give it more curve and
upward movement by cutting out a candle-flame-shaped piece of clay and
reattaching the seam by scoring and slipping. [I] While it is firming up,
work on the handle.

Curve the larger piece of clay cut from the Handle Template. The
stronger the curve, the more it will stick out away from the body of the
juicer. Play with the shape to see what you enjoy. Add the tiny strip along
the wall. Puff out the top piece with your fingers, and then slip and score it
in place. [J] Compress the seams with a soft rib.





  Now back to the spout. Blend in a cone of clay to the place where the
spout meets the wall. This strengthens the joint and visually connects the
spout to the wall in a more fluid way. [K]

Finishing Touches
Smooth, smooth, smooth! Don’t forget the underside, either. I suggest
cutting a beveled edge along the bottom. Work all the way around the edge
of the foot and the underside of the reamer attachment. [L] Use a wet
scouring pad first to take down corners and then finish up with a soft
sponge.

PROJECT:
              Teapot

When you make teapots, there are many relationships to consider. How will
the spout attach? Does the handle feel comfortable? Here we’ll explore
spouts made with soft slabs, using calipers to fit the lid, and making the
body out of wheel-thrown and slab-built parts. It is quite a puzzle!
   Thinking about how the liquid will flow from the spout is key. The
length and angle of the spout are significant factors. Placing the pouring end
of your spout just above the waterline is a good place to start. If the spout is
any lower, the liquid will come pouring out, even when you are not tipping
the pot forward.
    I encourage you to make extra lids, spouts, and handles in different sizes
so you can play with the relationships between them. Also, when you trim
the lid or place a handle there may be causalities. Extra parts provide
additional options.
    It takes careful attention to finish a teapot. There are many edges and
seams that require fine-tuning. Take the time to really refine the edge of the
spout. Recompress seams. Sand a little material from the lid’s edge if the fit
is too tight. Taking the time to consider of all these details will make your
work sing!

basic tool kit
body: 11/4 lb. (567 g) of clay
lid: 1/2 lb. (227 g) of clay
spout: slab that is 1/8" (3 mm) thick
strap handle: 7" long × 3/4" wide × 1/2" (18 cm × 2 cm × 1.3 cm) thick
bisque mold, shaped as shown here
diameters of 9" and 3" (23 cm and 7.5 cm), And a height of 3" (7.5 cm)
Teapot Foot Template, cut from 3/8" (1 cm) thick slab
Teapot Spout Template
small cone of leather-hard clay (knob) 1/2" × 1/2" (1.3 cm × 1.3 cm)
calipers
mandrel
water or slip for attachments
bat
foam bat

Instructions

Throwing the Body of the Teapot
Center the clay. Open it all the way down to the bat and widen it until you
reach an approximate diameter of 6" (15 mm). Pull the walls, taking care to
retain a thick rim. The rim needs to be thick in order to accommodate the
gallery, the ridge on the rim where the lid rests.
   Pull the walls up, keeping the rim narrower than the base. Once you have
the height—shoot for 4" (10 cm) tall—split the rim. This is the first step in
establishing the gallery. Providing support with one hand on either side,

press down in the center of the inner half of the rim with the corner of a
firm rib, creating the gallery ridge. [A]





  Once you have the gallery in place, work on refining the curve of the
wall. Press into the interior sidewall, developing a curve on the bottom two-
thirds of the cylinder. While you are pressing outward, support the outside
with a rib. This stretches the clay and also compresses it as the tea pot
widens. Use a rib to define the change in direction at the shoulder of the
teapot. Measure the diameter of the gallery with calipers while it is still
slowly spinning on the wheel. [B]

Throwing the Lid
Before you begin the lid, imagine the curve you want it to have. A visually
pleasing goal is to create a curve in the lid that completes the curve of the
body.
  You will be throwing the lid upside down. Begin by centering 1/2 lb.
(227 g) of clay. Measure with the calipers early on so you can visualize the
end diameter ahead of time. Form an initial small bowl shape by opening
the clay and pulling small walls. Measure again with the calipers. Make
sure to retain some thickness on the rim while you widen the walls and
develop the curve. Keep in mind that lids are a heavy-use item, and a
durable rim is important. Once you are close to the right diameter, pull it
just a touch wider. Then use a soft rib to flatten the outside of the lid’s edge.
[C] Measure again and again until it is very, very close. A little big is better,
as you can trim or sand off a little for a tight fit.

The Foot
Press the slab from the Foot Template onto the mold (see here). [D] Spin it
on the banding wheel as you press the center into the depression of the
mold with wet fingers. Compress the slab to the mold everywhere using a
soft rib. Let it dry on the mold until it is a soft leather-hard.

Combining the Pieces
Before you trim the top of the lid, check the fit. If it is a bit big, you may re-
center it oriented the way you threw it (upside down) and shave off clay
from the diameter. If all is well, center the lid with the excess clay facing
up, and trim away the clay to create a rounded dome. [E] Check for even
thickness and keep trimming until you achieve it.

To cut the teapot body off the bat, first place the lid in the gallery. (The
lid helps keep the gallery round as you alter the body.) Use your palms to
press in on opposite sides of the base, creating two points. [F] Invert the
teapot on a foam bat. Halfway between the points, begin to cut into the
teapot body, arching slowly down toward the pointed end. Match this with a
cut on the other side, removing an arching triangle of clay that dips about
3/4" (2 cm) into the body of the teapot. [G] This is where the point of the slab
foot will fit to the body. Repeat this cut on the other pointed end. Check to
make sure the slab foot fits. Trim the body so that it easily touches across
the curve of the slab. Slip and score these edges together. [H] Compress the
seam with a firm rib. On the inside, compress the seam with the end of a
long-handled paintbrush. Use the firm bristles to clean up excess slip and
smooth the seam. [I]

Finishing Touches
A mandrel is a really helpful tool for curving small slabs of clay for spouts
or handles. With this technique, you sandwich the clay between your rib
and mandrel. To round the clay, simply lay it on the mandrel, dip the edge
of your flexible rib in water (so it slides), and gently press down. You can
purchase wooden mandrels, or you can fashion one from clay, bisque fire it,
and use it to shape your spouts.

Making the Spout
Now for the spout! Place the template on the spout slab and cut out the
outer shape only (not the dart in the center). Cut the sides at a bevel so that
when you attach them they overlap. Round the slab on a mandrel, then
compress the seam inside and out with a narrow wooden tool and firm rib.
Hold it up to your teapot to gauge the height and the curve to work toward.
Trim the wide end where it will attach to fit the contour of the teapot. Trim
the tip to the height that works well for your form. [J]

If you want to increase the curve of the spout, cut the dart with beveled
edges. [K] Before you score it together, lightly close the opening and see if
you like it. If it’s still not quite right, trim a bit more. Score the attaching
edges and recompress the seam. Your spout should be leather-hard before
you attach it, otherwise you run the risk of deforming it when you press it
into place.





  Hold your spout up to the teapot and trace a line around where it will
attach. Punch the holes through the teapot and smooth the rough edges with
a sponge on the interior and exterior. [L] Score the attaching edges and very
gently press the spout into place. Compress and smooth around the seam.
Take time to refine and taper the edge of the spout. Thin and smooth the
edge of the spout with a wet scouring pad. Draw it repeatedly from the base
of the spout toward the edge. [M]

Finishing the Knob and Handle
For the knob on the lid, take the small cone of leather-hard clay you have
prepared and rasp a flat spot on the point. If you desire more of an oval
shape, shave off clay from the sides. Smooth it completely before you slip
and score the knob into place on the lid.
  Curve your soft leather-hard strap handle and trim the ends to fit to the
teapot. [N] Slip and score the ends into place. Recompress and smooth the
seams as described shown here. Drape plastic over your teapot and let it
dry.

Marty Fielding, on Process
                             www.martyfielding.com

Marty Fielding became captivated by clay as an anthropology major at the
University of North Carolina at Greensboro. He continued his study of
ceramics as a student and teaching assistant at Penland School of Craft. He
received an MFA from the University of Florida. He has taught locally and
as far away as the University of Georgia Studio Abroad in Cortona, Italy.
His work has been included in invitational and juried exhibitions nationally
and internationally. Learn more about his work in publications such as
Ceramics Monthly and Pottery Making Illustrated.

Can you tell us a bit about your process?
My process begins with a slab of red clay and a variety of templates. Many of the basic
forms start as a cylinder or a cone that is altered into a rectangle, trapezoid, etc. Each
piece is constructed by joining the basic forms and adding appendages such as handles,
spouts, and lids. I use two-part drop molds and press molds for some handles and spouts. I
approach the surface as if the piece is a 3D color field painting. I build up color by applying
thin layers of underglaze with the desire that brush strokes are visible and the lower layers
of color are visible in places. Transparent glaze is applied to select areas of the exteriors. I
fire to cone 3 in both electric and soda kilns.

What are a few of your inﬂuences?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe stated, “Music is liquid architecture; Architecture is frozen
music.” I explore how color harmony can reference tonal harmony to produce mood,
rhythm, and atmospheric effects akin to music.
     I draw from divergent sources that share the element of abstraction, an austerity and
restraint in form, and an intentional trajectory for moving the body, eye, or psyche through
space. Grounded architecturally inspired forms communicate stability, and cantilevered
components act as a counterpoint to the mass. Visual chords of color establish a
comforting harmonized background. Architectural features punctuated with vivid color
conduct the viewer’s eye around the piece and settle into a mellow mid-tempo beat.
  Geometric forms combined with color become utilitarian 3D color field paintings.
Individual vessels and function-specific sets reference skyline and double as musical
phrasing or waveforms of sound. Both architects and potters are fundamentally engaged in

designing functional space. Architecture holds people; people hold pottery. Like the
sentiment in a song, I instill calmness in my vessels to be experienced through use and
contemplation within people’s hands and homes.

PROJECT:
               Oil Pourer

This little oil pourer is fully composed of slabs shaped on bisque molds. A
tapered narrow spout is perfect for controlling the pour of oil, vinegar, or
soy sauce. Try out this elegant form and test your handbuilding skills using
bisque molds, templates, and multiple slab parts.
  The upper and lower sections of the oil pourer are each made of two
pieces that clamshell together. It is an engaging combination of shapes.
Since the project relies on multiple bisque molds and templates, each
person’s version will vary. Part of the joy of making your own tools is that
they will impart your touch and ideas to the clay.

Tools & Materials
basic tool kit
Oil Pourer Bottom Template, cut from fresh clay
2 Oil Pourer Top Templates, cut from fresh clay
Oil Pourer Upper Half Template A, cut from fresh clay
Oil Pourer Upper Half Template B (cut from fresh clay
Oil Pourer Long Spout Template, from a 1/8" (3mm) thick soft leather-hard slab
water or slip for attachments

Instructions
Shape the Bottom, Top, and Upper Half (A and B) Templates on bisque
molds. For the upper halves, you can perforate the templates on the dashed
center lines and use this as a guide for placement on your mold. See the top
image shown here for an example of this. Let them dry until they are
leather-hard.
  Shave the edges of the Upper halves. Hold them stacked and see if the
edges align. Trim away more clay if needed until they will attach cleanly.
[A] Slip and score the edges and combine the two pieces into an enclosed
form. Use a firm rib to compress the edge where they meet. This shape will
become the top portion of the pourer.

Repeat this process with the pieces of the lower portion of the body
shaped by the two Top Template pieces. They will become the top half of
the lower portion of the pouring vessel. Trim, score, and attach the two
pieces together. [B] Compress the interior and exterior of the seam. Shape
the Bottom Template as shown here. Trim the halves of the lower section.
Clam shell together the pieces that compose the enclosed lower portion of
the body. [C]

Before stacking the upper halves and bottom section, trim the rim in a
pleasing curve. Visually center the upper section. Trace around its base,
marking a line onto the bottom section. Cut about 1/4" (6 mm) inside this
line and remove the clay. Score both sections and attach them together.
Compress the seam on the outside with the corner of a firm rib. [D]





  Add a little wedge of clay at the foot. This acts like a bike kickstand and
increases the stability of the pot while it is on the table. Start with a tapered
half-moon of clay. Place the enclosed form on your work surface. After
scoring, press the moon shape so that it wedges against the clay and surface
of the table. [E] Remove it and keep the bottom section covered in plastic
while it dries to leather-hard. Then use a rasp to clarify the shape. Double
check that it still fits into place. Smooth the surface then slip and score it
into place. Compress around the seam.

Lightly cover the body while you work on making the spout. Take the
clay shaped by the Spout Template and bevel the edges so they will overlap
when they connect. Bend the slab around a tapered wooden mandrel to
create an even curve, then compress the seam. [F] Remove the slab and
orient it vertically. Slip and score the edges and compress the exterior of the
seam against them with a soft rib.

Trim the spout to fit the body. Trace around the base of the spout to mark
where the spout will attach. Cut 1/4" (6 mm) inside this line and remove the
circular shape. Score the edges and press the spout into place. Be careful
not to dent the spout when you press it into place. [G]

Add a coil to the edge of the rim to strengthen seams and add visual
rhythm. [H] Use a rasp, wet scouring pad, and sponge to remove any
unwanted marks and smooth the surface of the oil pourer (more details
shown here).

Variation for a Handbuilt Lid and Gallery
If you would prefer to handbuild a lid, there is a way! Scale up your oil
pourer into a teapot and make this lid to go along with it. The lid
templates are made to fit a larger pot. Enlarge your oil pourer templates
by 25 percent to fit this lid.

Tools & Materials
basic tool kit
gallery bisque mold
Oil Pourer Lid Template A
3" × 3" soft leather-hard slab 3/8" (1 cm) thick
Oil Pourer Lid Templates B, C, and D from a soft leather-hard
   slab 3/8" (1 cm) thick

Instructions
Insert a horizontal plain (or gallery) to hold a lid in place before
attaching the upper section to the lower section. This can be a flat piece
of clay with a hole cut in it, or you may fashion a bisque mold to shape
the slab with a circular gallery for a lid. To find the shape of the gallery,
trim Template A to fit the interior contour of the upper section. Once it
fits, mark a line on the interior of the upper section where the gallery
will be scored into place. [A]

Use a bisque mold to create a gallery. Lay a slab on it, and, with the
mold spinning on a banding wheel, depress the slab to take on the
contour of the mold. Cut a circle into the gallery on which the lid can
rest. Once it is a soft leather-hard, use your trimmed template to fit the
gallery into the upper section.
  Round the ends of Template D into a flange for the lid. Trim its
circumference to fit inside the opening of the gallery. Use Template A
as a starting point to shape the plain of the gallery so that it can be
inserted into the upper portion of the vessel. Make a cone out of
Template B for the roof of the lid. Using a 3/8" (1 cm) thick slab and
starting with Template C as a guide, trim a circle of clay that fits inside
the gallery. Slip and score the three pieces of the lid together. Insert and
attach the gallery. Slip and score a coil along the seam and blend it into
place. [B] Complete the lid by compressing the seams, smoothing the
surface, and adding a knob of your choice! Refine and smooth the
edges and seams. [C]

Acknowledgments
With each morning coffee, I am reminded of the people who have made my
journey as a potter possible. A few of them are on the cup shelf pictured
here, and there are so many more! I developed a whole new level of stamina
while writing this book, and leaned on so many people throughout the
process!
  I’m grateful for role models within my family. My Oma, who tirelessly
tended her garden. She widened the circle of family to every friend through
delicious meals and letters. My Opa, a small shoe shop owner,
demonstrated the joy of taking lunch at home and striking up conversation
with customers. As immigrants, they creatively forged a path for their
family.
   Dad, you taught me to be mesmerized by raindrops on spiderwebs and to
have keen attention while combing for shells on long beach walks. Mom!
You have always positioned yourself directly in my corner. I’ve counted on
you to help me move across the country how many times? You encouraged
me to shoot for my dreams! You both taught me to love material, whether it
was crayons, fabric, wood, or flour. Sister, your resilience, gorgeous food
photos, and healing touch add so much to my life!
  Thank you to my professors and mentors for the amazing academic and
hands-on learning experiences. Each of you gifted me with knowledge and
support. I’m so grateful I get to chase after this crazy life as a potter.
  Thank you to my partner Joe Wilkinson for riding this roller coaster life
with me. When life feels overwhelming (like when I am writing a book,
teaching internationally, prepping for craft fairs… oh, and trying to make
pottery), he helps me keep perspective and stay light-hearted. He organized
the collective purchase of a new computer for my fortieth birthday with a
bunch of friends and family! You all saved me countless hours of watching
the “spinning rainbow wheel of death” on my ten-year-old laptop. You gave
me a tool that lightens the load of many projects, namely this one!
  Keeping the wheels turning at the studio would never happen without the
incredible help of my studio assistants—past and present. Each person has
contributed in a powerful way. From amazing studio signs, to building
shelves, from developing new classes to dialing specific gravity procedures,
from delicious group lunches, to spreading mulch, and from beers out in the
evening to making studio events flow smoothly—you all rock my world.

You have helped me grow personally and helped tend to the studio
physically and energetically. Thank you, thank you, thank you!
   Matisse Lorance Berthiaume, photographer extraordinaire, you captured
each and every detail in the perfect light. Thank you for the countless hours
shooting and thoughtful suggestions. Your unbelievable attention to detail
amazes me!
   Josh DeWeese, you have inspired me for years! Thank you for writing
the forward. And a special thank you to all the artist contributors. It’s been
fun corresponding with you and gathering your inspirational work and

  Thanks to my editor Thom O’Hearn for his encouragement, editing, and

About the Author
DEB SCHWARTZKOPF is a studio potter, instructor, and active community
member in Seattle, Washington. She has taught at Ohio University,
Massachusetts College of Art and Design, University of Washington, and
University of Georgia’s study abroad program in Cortona. She was named
Ceramics Monthly and Ceramic Arts Daily’s 2019 Artist of the Year, one of
the most visible awards in the field. Deb has worked as an artist in
residence nationally and internationally at the Archie Bray Foundation
(MT), Mudflat Studios (MA), The Clay Studio (PA), Pottery Northwest
(WA), Watershed (ME), Red Lodge Clay Studio, (MT) Sanbao in
Jingdezhen, China, and the Center for Ceramics in Berlin, Germany.
   Since 2002, Deb has also taught widely at top ceramics centers including
Penland School of Craft, Gaya Ceramics Arts Center (Indonesia), and IARE
(France). Her artwork is included in collections such as The Rosenfield
Collection, the Kamm Teapot Foundation, San Angelo Museum of Fine
Arts, and the Washington State Arts Commission, among others. She has
been included in numerous publications including What Makes a Potter:
Functional Pottery in America, Ceramic Monthly, Pottery Making
Illustrated, and Studio Potter magazine; has contributed to Tales of a Red
Clay Rambler podcasts; has served as the director of the Washington Clay
Arts Association; and is currently a board member at Pottery Northwest. In
2013, Deb founded and launched what is now Rat City Studios, a
community pottery studio where she offers adult classes, studio
memberships, and opportunities for emerging artists: ratcitystudios.com.
